4453: Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in the Solar System. Its summit stands roughly 22 km above the surrounding Martian plains, yet its shield spreads roughly 600 km across. Much of the climb is surprisingly gentle. The abrupt break comes at the foot. Trace the cliff around its base and look beyond it for the debris left where parts of the flank collapsed.
ESA · At the foot of Olympus Mons
4454: This is the cliff at the edge of Olympus Mons. It marks a startling change in slope after the long, shallow descent from the summit. Beyond the cliff lie enormous, hummocky deposits. Mars Express images help connect those deposits to landslides that carried pieces of the volcanic flank out across the plains.
6288: Valles Marineris stretches about 4,000 km along the Martian equator. In places the canyon system reaches about 7 km deep. From high above, trace its branches eastward from the Tharsis rise. Descend into a single trough and the walls conceal most of the system that was visible from orbit.
14300: A river once entered a lake inside Jezero and dropped sediment as it slowed. The deposit built outward into a delta. Its surviving layers give Perseverance a place to investigate ancient environments and collect samples of material carried into the crater from the surrounding watershed.
2071: Gale preserves a record of water in the middle of an impact crater. Curiosity found rocks deposited by streams and lakes near the foot of Mount Sharp. Climbing the mountain lets the rover read successively higher layers, sampling a history that erosion has exposed in cross section.
NASA · Water and sediment in Gale
15000: Aeolis Mons is the layered mountain inside Gale crater that the Curiosity team calls Mount Sharp. Its position matters as much as its height. A traverse uphill takes the rover through different sedimentary layers, allowing it to compare the environments in which those layers formed.
NASA · Sedimentation and erosion in Gale
2432: Hellas Planitia occupies the floor of a giant impact basin in the southern highlands. Orbiting laser altimeters made its scale unmistakable. Follow a route from the highlands down to the plain to see how an impact can reshape an entire region of a planet.
3550: Maat Mons is a volcano under Venus's cloud deck. Magellan used radar to trace long lava flows across the plains at its base. The familiar perspective view of the mountain was constructed from radar imagery and measurements of elevation, giving us a landscape no ordinary orbital camera could see through the clouds.
NASA · Magellan's view of Maat Mons
3766: Maxwell Montes contains the highest terrain on Venus. Its mountains rise beside the high plain of Lakshmi Planum. Much of the range shines in Magellan radar images. Partway up the range, look for Cleopatra, a circular impact crater interrupting the mountain terrain.
979: Caloris Planitia lies inside one of Mercury's great impact basins, roughly 1,550 km across. The collision excavated the basin, and volcanic plains later covered much of its interior. MESSENGER's color maps help distinguish those plains from the material around the basin rim.
3691: The Sea of Tranquility is a dark plain of ancient basalt. Its southwestern part became the setting for Apollo 11 in July 1969. From Earth, the whole mare is visible in a small telescope. The landing site occupies a tiny patch of what looks, at that distance, like a single smooth plain.
5684: Tranquility Base marks the Apollo 11 landing. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle here on July 20, 1969, while Michael Collins orbited above. The first samples people collected on another world came from this part of the Sea of Tranquility.
6163: Near full Moon, Tycho is easier to find by its rays than by its rim. Bright streaks of ejecta spread far across the lunar surface from the impact site. Under lower sunlight the view changes. The crater walls and the central mountain stand out in shadow while the rays become less conspicuous.
3685: Mare Orientale is the dark plain in the center of a much larger impact structure. An overhead view reveals concentric mountain rings around the plain. From Earth we see the basin almost edge-on, so spacecraft gave us a far clearer picture of the rings and how a giant impact reshaped the lunar crust.
NASA · The history of Orientale basin
5707: Stickney is so large in proportion to Phobos that its rim changes the silhouette of the moon. A second, smaller crater lies inside it. Looking across Stickney from a low angle gives a sense of how little room there is for an impact of this size on such a small, irregular body.
3459: Loki Patera contains a vast lava lake. Juno observations revealed a remarkably smooth surface with islands within it. Infrared measurements are especially revealing here. They can pick out hot material along the edges even when much of the lake has acquired a cooler crust.
1282: Conamara Chaos looks like a puzzle whose pieces have shifted. Blocks of Europa's striped ice sit at different orientations in a rougher matrix. Compare the line patterns on neighboring blocks. They preserve a record of movement within the icy shell after those stripes originally formed.
NASA · Landscapes and features of Europa
6284: Valhalla records a giant impact into Callisto's icy surface. A relatively bright center is surrounded by a succession of low rings that extend far beyond it. Pull back until several rings are visible together. Their shared center is easier to recognize from orbit than along any one arc at ground level.
2478: Herschel is about 130 km wide on a moon less than 400 km across. The central peak rises from the crater floor and the walls are several kilometers high. In a full view of Mimas, this single impact interrupts so much of the facing hemisphere that the crater is recognizable even at a distance.
14248: Baghdad Sulcus is one of the south polar fractures nicknamed the tiger stripes. Cassini measured heat along the fracture, and jets in this polar region feed the plume above Enceladus. The bright surface seen in ordinary images and the warmth measured in infrared reveal different aspects of the same active landscape.
NASA · The warmth of Baghdad Sulcus
4406: Odysseus spans nearly two-fifths of the diameter of Tethys. Its floor follows much of the moon's round outline. Over time, icy terrain can relax under gravity, softening the relief of a huge impact even while its circular perimeter remains recognizable from orbit.
6026: Tirawa is one of Rhea's great impact basins. Compare it with Mamaldi. Later craters interrupt their outlines, allowing observers to work out which impacts happened after the basins had already formed.
14400: Ligeia Mare is a sea of liquid hydrocarbons near Titan's north pole. Cassini radar images taken on different flybys showed a bright feature appearing and changing within the normally dark sea. The nickname “magic island” describes its shifting appearance. Its identity was a question for the observations to test.
1047: Cassini Regio makes up much of the dark side of two-toned Iapetus. Dark ground absorbs more sunlight, helping water ice escape and collect in colder, brighter areas. That feedback can sharpen an initial difference in color into the striking contrast seen from space.
6587: Wunda contains a bright ring that stands out on the otherwise dark, heavily cratered face of Umbriel. Voyager 2 saw it during the 1986 flyby. Brightness is the firmest clue here. The limited views leave the nature and history of the bright material open to interpretation.
2340: Dark material covers part of the floor of Hamlet, while the rays outside this impact crater stand out brightly on Oberon. These contrasts were recorded during Voyager 2's brief encounter with Uranus. The composition of the dark deposit is less certain than its outline in the images.
15669: Sputnik Planitia is the bright western lobe of Pluto's heart. A thick glacier dominated by nitrogen ice fills the basin. Its surface is divided into broad cells. Slow circulation within the ice carries material upward and back down, renewing the surface and helping explain the scarcity of visible impact craters.
15736: Kubrick Mons is one of Charon's mountains surrounded by a depression. New Horizons images show an isolated high block with a moat-like outline around its foot. The unusual pairing of a mountain and a hollow is the observation that theories of its formation must explain.
5789: Jonathan Swift sent Gulliver to meet astronomers who described two small moons of Mars. Swift published that story in 1726, more than a century before Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and Deimos in 1877. One of the few named craters on the smaller moon now carries the author's name.
6431: This crater honors Voltaire, who gave Mars two moons in his story Micromégas decades before anyone saw the real pair. Deimos also has a crater named Swift, honoring another writer who imagined the same number. The literary connection explains why these two names appear together on such a small moon.
2076: Galileo Regio preserves some of Ganymede's ancient dark terrain. Galileo spacecraft images resolve old impact craters and deep furrows in its ice-rich crust. Compare the region with the brighter belts of grooved terrain nearby. On one moon, they preserve strikingly different histories of resurfacing.
NASA · Ancient impacts in Galileo Regio
4638: Pele paints a broad red deposit around its volcanic center on Io. Material thrown up in a plume falls back to the surface over a much larger area than the vent itself. Galileo observations tracked changes in the deposit, giving scientists a record of activity between visits.
14384: Padua Chasmata belongs to Dione's network of deep fractures. In Voyager images this side of the moon looked streaked with bright wisps. Cassini's closer views resolved icy cliffs, turning what had looked like a pattern painted on the surface into evidence that the crust had broken.
2879: Kachina Chasmata is the largest named canyon system on Ariel by cataloged span. Pull back far enough to follow its course before looking across its walls. Canyons on this moon record a time when the crust stretched and broke, interrupting an already cratered surface.
3870: Messina Chasmata traces a major system of fault valleys on Titania. Voyager 2 saw valleys cutting the icy surface in different directions. The pattern is evidence that the crust stretched. An overhead view shows how far the fractures run, while a low view emphasizes their walls.
6359: Verona Rupes is an immense cliff on Miranda. Voyager 2 recorded it near the edge of the illuminated surface in 1986. The view makes its shadow dramatic but complicates the measurement of its true height, one reason different estimates are quoted for this scarp.
2504: Hili marks one of the active plumes discovered on Triton during the Voyager 2 flyby. The plume rose from the bright southern terrain and bent downwind at altitude. Its shape provided evidence of both activity at the surface and winds in Triton's thin atmosphere.
